note: What a scrolling list states about itself so the layout, and not us, divides the height. Three shapes were tried in each product and each patched the one before: a height written in the panel, a share worked out in proportion to the rows, then that share computed from an ESTIMATE of the available room — settled once, at draw time, inside layout engines that know the real sizes and re-run on every resize. A list now says its whole content (a ceiling, never a wish), the least it can be squeezed to, and nothing else; the surface says what those floors cost it, which is the minimum size it must refuse to go below.

whole.out: number: everything it holds, chrome included

least.out: number: the smallest box still worth showing

least_measured.out: number: the same floor, for a caller that measured the whole instead of adding it up

least_surface.out: number: the minimum height the surface holding them must declare

cases.why: a ceiling: a list handed more than it holds draws a gap under its last row while the list beside it is still scrolling
a list being refilled holds nothing for a frame, and an empty one is a sentence rather than a scroll area
one row shows that a list exists, two show that it is a list — and a floor counted in rows alone did not cover the heading
a floor larger than what the list holds is the gap under the last row, arrived at from the other side
how far a list may be squeezed does not depend on how much it holds; who gets cut first does, and that is what the whole says
a measured whole answers the same floor as a declared one — the chrome is whatever it turned out to be, and is never given up
a list already shorter than the floor is at its floor; taking a row off it would be taking the list
🔴 the reason this exists: the two cards of one window differ by thirty pixels of heading, so one declared figure for both cut the taller list short or padded the shorter one
the window could be shrunk past both floors, so the second list went under the docked bar and covered the Close button
a list shorter than the floor costs only what it holds, so a screen is not made to reserve room for rows that do not exist
